scenes.visual: Title card 'Fewer Pores' fades in over a greenhouse bench of young barley plants, 16:9. Same colour map as the first film. COLOUR MAP, same in every scene and in the second film: carbon dioxide = TEAL arrows; water vapour = BLUE arrows; oxygen = WARM RED arrows; guard cells and stomata = PURPLE; 'the price' (water lost per gas gained) = a GOLD balance scale; waxy layer, cells and labels = GREY. Leaf A = solid outline, leaf B = dashed outline. Cartoon schematics only, no molecular structures; every bar or gauge not computed is labelled 'schematic'. Numbers appear only as on-screen text.

scenes.tts: If you remove most of a barley leaf's pores, does the plant go hungry? Or can it save water and still fill its grain?
scenes.visual: A cartoon barley leaf surface dotted with PURPLE stomata. Most of the dots fade away. Beside it, a barley head with grains, a question mark over it. Question card: 'Fewer pores: a hungry plant?'
scenes.narration: If you remove most of a barley leaf's pores, does the plant go hungry? Or can it save water and still fill its grain?

scenes.tts: On paper, a leaf with fewer pores can pay less water for its carbon. A real experiment tested what fewer pores do to a crop.
scenes.visual: Leaf A (solid outline) and leaf B (dashed outline) side by side, leaf B with fewer PURPLE pores; the GOLD scale beside leaf B tips less steeply. Text: 'leaf B was made up'. Then both leaves dissolve into a greenhouse bench.
scenes.narration: On paper, a leaf with fewer pores can pay less water for its carbon. A real experiment tested what fewer pores do to a crop.

scenes.tts: Julie Gray's team, with Hughes as first author, worked in barley. They made plants overexpress a barley gene, H V E P F one. That means making extra of the gene's product.
scenes.caption: Julie Gray's team, with Hughes as first author, worked in barley. They made plants overexpress a barley gene, HvEPF1. That means making extra of the gene's product.
scenes.visual: Labelled block 'HvEPF1 gene' slides into a cartoon plant cell; many small copies of a labelled block 'HvEPF1 product' pour out. Credit text: 'Hughes, Gray and colleagues, Plant Physiology, 2017'.
scenes.narration: Julie Gray's team, with Hughes as first author, worked in barley. They made plants overexpress a barley gene, HvEPF1. That means making extra of the gene's product.

scenes.tts: This gene limits leaf cells from entering stomatal development and moving through it. So extra product should mean fewer stomata. They compared these plants with empty-vector controls.
scenes.visual: A row of young GREY leaf cells; arrows show a few heading toward becoming PURPLE stomata, while HvEPF1 blocks stop most of them. A control plant appears beside the engineered plants, labelled 'empty-vector control: same procedure, no added gene'.
scenes.narration: This gene limits leaf cells from entering stomatal development and moving through it. So extra product should mean fewer stomata. They compared these plants with empty-vector controls.

scenes.tts: Leaf surface impressions told the story. Two engineered lines kept only about a quarter and an eighth of the controls' stomata.
scenes.visual: Dental resin is pressed onto a leaf and peeled off; clear varnish is painted onto the resin mould; the varnish copy is peeled from the resin and goes under a cartoon microscope. Three fields of view: control dense with PURPLE dots; line 1 with far fewer; line 2 sparser still. On-screen labels: 'about 24%' and 'about 12%' of control density, 'mature sixth leaf'.
scenes.narration: Leaf surface impressions told the story. Two engineered lines kept only about a quarter and an eighth of the controls' stomata.

scenes.tts: Why the controls, and why two lines? The procedure itself might change a leaf. And the inserted gene lands somewhere in the genome. Two independent lines make a landing-spot effect less likely.
scenes.visual: Three plants in a row: 'empty-vector control', 'line 1', 'line 2'. A GREY procedure icon (a labelled 'vector' block carrying DNA) passes over all three. A cartoon chromosome for each line shows the gene block landing at a different spot, labelled 'insertion site differs'.
scenes.narration: Why the controls, and why two lines? The procedure itself might change a leaf. And the inserted gene lands somewhere in the genome. Two independent lines make a landing-spot effect less likely.

scenes.tts: Next, a leaf was clamped in a small chamber that measures gas exchange. In well-watered plants, leaves with fewer stomata exchanged much less gas with the air.
scenes.visual: A small cartoon clamp-on chamber closes over an attached leaf; air flows in and out through tubes. A GREY gauge labelled 'gas exchange (stomatal conductance)' falls for the engineered leaf (dashed outline) compared with the control leaf beside it (solid outline). TEAL and BLUE arrow streams both thin, labelled 'schematic consequence of lower conductance, not a reported transpiration comparison'.
scenes.narration: Next, a leaf was clamped in a small chamber that measures gas exchange. In well-watered plants, leaves with fewer stomata exchanged much less gas with the air.

scenes.tts: Gas exchange fell steeply. So what happened to the carbon taken in, and to the grain? Did they fall just as steeply?
scenes.visual: Two empty bar slots appear: 'carbon gained' and 'grain yield', each with a question mark, beside the lowered gas-exchange gauge. Question card: 'Did carbon and grain fall as steeply?'
scenes.narration: Gas exchange fell steeply. So what happened to the carbon taken in, and to the grain? Did they fall just as steeply?

scenes.visual: Question card holds; a small timer ring fills.

scenes.tts: In general, if fewer pores slow gas flow while photosynthesis continues, carbon dioxide inside the leaf falls. Its gap widens, and that props up carbon gain. So a leaf can save more water than it loses carbon. In this study, one efficiency measure rose in both lines under water restriction. The measures did not all agree.
scenes.visual: Back on the leaf: the inside TEAL gauge drops, and the TEAL 'CO2 gap' bar grows taller. The TEAL stream shrinks only a little while the BLUE stream shrinks a lot. Label: 'general physiology, schematic, not measured in this study'. The GOLD scale tips less steeply. Then a small panel: 'water-use efficiency (from leaf carbon isotopes), water restricted: up in both lines' with a GREY note 'measures did not all agree'.
scenes.narration: In general, if fewer pores slow gas flow while photosynthesis continues, carbon dioxide inside the leaf falls. Its gap widens, and that props up carbon gain. So a leaf can save more water than it loses carbon. In this study, one efficiency measure rose in both lines under water restriction. The measures did not all agree.

scenes.tts: And the grain? In a greenhouse trial, neither line showed a statistically significant drop in yield, well watered or water restricted. No drop was detected.
scenes.visual: Grain-yield bars for control, line 1 and line 2, in two groups labelled 'well watered' and 'water restricted'. Error bars overlap heavily. Label: 'no significant drop detected'. Bars marked 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: And the grain? In a greenhouse trial, neither line showed a statistically significant drop in yield, well watered or water restricted. No drop was detected.

scenes.tts: But each group held only five plants. A small loss could still hide below what the trial could see. No drop detected is not proof of equal yield.
scenes.visual: Five small plant icons sit under each bar. A faint dashed band below the control bar is labelled 'a small loss could hide here'. Stamp text: 'not proof of equal yield'.
scenes.narration: But each group held only five plants. A small loss could still hide below what the trial could see. No drop detected is not proof of equal yield.

scenes.tts: So what kind of answer is this? It shows how one gene limits stomata, and what fewer stomata do to gas, water and grain. It says nothing about why wild barley evolved its stomatal density.
scenes.visual: Screen splits in two. Left panel 'HOW': the HvEPF1 block stopping cells from becoming stomata, the gas chamber and the grain bars, filled in. Right panel 'WHY': a wild barley field and a small branching tree of grass lineages, left blank with a question mark.
scenes.narration: So what kind of answer is this? It shows how one gene limits stomata, and what fewer stomata do to gas, water and grain. It says nothing about why wild barley evolved its stomatal density.

scenes.tts: That second question is about lineages and their history, not one plant. Answering it needs different evidence, and it is where the lesson goes next.
scenes.visual: The blank 'WHY' panel grows to fill the screen; branches of the tree light up one after another, a GREY question mark at the root.
scenes.narration: That second question is about lineages and their history, not one plant. Answering it needs different evidence, and it is where the lesson goes next.

scenes.visual: Hex end card. Take-home line: 'Fewer pores can save more water than they cost in carbon.'
